system: You rewrite research decisions as topic-neutral abstractions. Return only the JSON object asked for.
prompt:
Below are research decisions made by several different researchers. Rewrite each one so that a reader
cannot tell what field, subfield, topic, paper, organisation or person it comes from, but can still see the research
trade-off that was faced and which way it was decided.

For each item return:
- "abstract_problem": the decision problem as a generic research trade-off (one or two sentences, at most 40 words).
- "abstract_choice": what was chosen, over what alternative when one is given, and the stated reason if any (one or
  two sentences, at most 45 words). Start it with "Chose to".

Rules:
- Remove every domain noun and technical term: names of models, systems, datasets, benchmarks, methods,
  organisations, people, papers, phenomena and coined terms; and any wording that reveals the area (for example
  AI, machine learning, language models, neural networks, training, fine-tuning, prompts, attacks, security,
  privacy, policy, labs, governments, biology).
- Use only generic research vocabulary: system, method, intervention, treatment, condition, measurement, signal,
  effect, baseline, control, sample, variant, procedure, dataset, outcome, claim, hypothesis, collaborator, audience.
- Keep the structure of the trade-off (for example speed vs rigour, breadth vs depth, a bold vs a hedged claim,
  a direct vs an indirect measurement, a natural vs a constructed setting, continue vs stop) and the direction chosen.
- Add nothing that is not in the source: no judgement, praise or new detail. Never say who made the decision.
- Write every item in the same plain style and at a similar length.

Return {"items": [{"id": ..., "abstract_problem": ..., "abstract_choice": ...}, ...]} with one entry per input
item, in input order.

ITEMS:
[
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:7ef189c8d0ce",
  "problem": "How strongly to claim that prompt wording affects cheating, and what to recommend to practitioners.",
  "did": "They ablated four prompts of varying strictness, found cheating rates swing widely while original-benchmark performance does not, and recommended careful prompt ablations before deployment.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "Prompts did not produce statistically significant differences on the original benchmarks, yet cheating rates differed greatly, with GPT-5 dropping from over 85% to 1% under the strictest prompt."
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:7ba49fb55ed1",
  "problem": "Which DPO iterate to use as the regularizer in Frank-Wolfe when the best-scoring iterate has very low entropy.",
  "did": "They used the 2nd of 15 DPO iterations as the regularizer for later rounds instead of the best-scoring iterate.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "the best DPO iterate by elicitation score"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "The best iterate sometimes has very low entropy, making it an ineffective regularizer, while the 2nd iterate uses a similar qualitative strategy with higher entropy."
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:db95081682bf",
  "problem": "RepE increased the log-likelihood difference in debiasing, which is an unexpected result needing explanation.",
  "did": "They interpreted it as RepE overshooting equality and hypothesized that bias is not linearly represented, while the decoder handles nonlinear concepts.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "A concept such as bias may not be linearly represented, yet RepE steers towards linear concepts."
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:a6ab44bbf18c",
  "problem": "How to organize the space of oversight research problems so that scalable objectives can be designed for each.",
  "did": "They built a 3x3 taxonomy crossing question types (what happened, could happen, why) with data sources (behaviors, representations, data) and pursued all cells together.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "building local solutions for individual tasks"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Progress on the questions compounds, since data from one cell feeds others, giving reason for optimism that oversight progress will accelerate."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:0abebebd11b3",
  "problem": "Choosing an evaluation set that tests detection against attacks that existing defenses cannot catch.",
  "did": "They built a set of 8 adversarial and 5 benign fine-tunes in which each adversarial datapoint is individually harmless, covering diverse attack types, and included challenging benign cases.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "The set is meant to be challenging: adversarial data bypasses content moderation, and benign fine-tunes (low-resource language, etc.) can have unintentional side effects that look mildly harmful."
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:2a3759f67dd6",
  "problem": "How to interpret the weaker performance of white-box methods on the direct evaluation set.",
  "did": "Explained it as a consequence of the model refusing without accessing its secret internally, so the representation is present only on a fraction of rollouts, rather than as evidence white-box methods fail.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "On direct prompts the secret-keeping model can refuse without needing to access its secret knowledge internally, especially in the Taboo case."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:4d3436db4963",
  "problem": "How to rule out that a student's gain in letter counting comes from the fine-tuning process itself",
  "did": "Added a control student trained with the same prompts, hyperparameters and seed on answers from the base model.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "The two datasets differ only in whether a model finetuned on letter counting wrote the responses."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:24f85b4d1639",
  "problem": "How to keep the evaluation signal on the trained fixation clean, so that bee/crow content in outputs isn't just an echo of the prohibition text.",
  "did": "Chose each prohibited item X to be concrete and relevant to the scenario but clearly unrelated to bees or crows.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "Not named explicitly. The implied alternative is a prohibition that could relate to bees or crows."
  ],
  "stated_reason": "So that the content judge's labels remain a clean signal of the trained fixation rather than an echo of the prohibition itself."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:1be80a47a676",
  "problem": "How strongly to state a claim",
  "did": "Overall cautious framing and caveats in text",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "Explicitly notes that ideas are not written with full research, are not highest priority, and should be taken with a grain of salt"
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:a871d2420363",
  "problem": "Whether homeopathic learning is specific to subliminal learning or a general phenomenon, and which settings to test it in",
  "did": "Tested homeopathic learning beyond subliminal learning: archaic bird names (no teacher), conditional misalignment from inoculation prompting, and an MNIST classifier",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "subliminal learning only",
   "settings without a teacher model or distillation"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Homeopathic learning might be specific to subliminal learning, so the authors tested it where there is no teacher or distillation."
 }
]
